standard.title: Analyse and visualise data
standard.description: Analyse and visualise data using a range of software, including spreadsheets and databases, to draw conclusions and make predictions by identifying trends
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can acquire, store and validate data from a range of sources (AC9TDI8P01). They have worked with data in spreadsheets but have not yet selected visualisation types, summarised data by attributes to identify trends, or drawn evidence-based conclusions and predictions.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students analyse and visualise data by choosing appropriate graph types and representations, summarise data by attributes to identify trends and patterns, and draw conclusions and make predictions supported by evidence from the data.

nodes.label: Choosing visualisation types
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can select an appropriate visualisation type (graph, chart, map, diagram) for a given dataset and explain why it suits the data
nodes.minimum_width: Given a dataset, choose a graph type and explain why it is appropriate for showing the pattern or relationship in the data
nodes.typical_width: Compare visualisation options for multidimensional data — explain why a scatter plot coloured by a third variable reveals more than a simple bar chart for the same data
wider: Investigate how visualisation choices can reveal or obscure patterns — compare two different graph types for the same dataset and explain what each makes visible and what it hides
Explore how social network diagrams or geographic maps reveal patterns that standard graphs cannot

response_modes.reason: Visualisation selection requires accumulating a repertoire of graph types and understanding what each makes visible. Students need enough examples to stop defaulting to bar charts — the repertoire is the prior condition for choosing appropriately.

nodes.hinge_reason: Students with only one or two graph types in their repertoire will default to the same type regardless of data structure. Nodes 2 and 3 require students to choose visualisations that reveal the relevant patterns — a thin repertoire produces graphs that obscure the trends they need to identify and conclude from.
success_criteria: Selects a visualisation type that is appropriate for the data structure (not just defaulting to one type)
Explains why the chosen type suits this particular dataset

nodes.label: Identifying trends and patterns
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can summarise data by attributes to identify trends, patterns and outliers
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least one trend or pattern in a visualised dataset; describe what the trend shows
nodes.typical_width: Summarise data by sorting or grouping by attributes; identify trends and at least one outlier; explain what the pattern means in context
wider: Compare trends identified manually with those generated by an AI model using natural language queries — do they find the same patterns?
Investigate how sorting crime data by type of offence reveals trends that raw data obscures
success_criteria: Identifies at least one trend or pattern in the data
Describes the trend in context (not just 'it goes up')

nodes.label: Drawing conclusions and making predictions
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can draw evidence-based conclusions from analysed data and make predictions by extending identified trends
nodes.minimum_width: State a conclusion supported by at least one piece of evidence from the data; make one prediction based on an identified trend
nodes.typical_width: Draw conclusions that reference multiple data points or patterns; make predictions and explain the reasoning; acknowledge limitations or uncertainty in the prediction
wider: Compare a predictive AI model's output against manually tagged data to evaluate its accuracy and effectiveness
Evaluate the confidence of a prediction — what would need to be true for the prediction to hold, and what could invalidate it?

response_modes.reason: Drawing conclusions requires students to distinguish between what the data shows, what it suggests, and what is uncertain. Scaffolding the reasoning structure (evidence → conclusion → prediction → limitation) prevents students from presenting opinion as data-supported conclusion.

Conclusions integrate visualisation selection (Node 1) and trend identification (Node 2) into evidence-based claims. Students who treat conclusion-drawing as separate from the prior analysis produce unsupported claims.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The AI comparison direction (comparing model output against manual analysis) is genuinely rich — it requires students to evaluate claims critically rather than accepting outputs, which goes meaningfully beyond making their own predictions.
success_criteria: States a conclusion that references specific evidence from the data
Makes a prediction that extends an identified trend
Does not present opinion as conclusion — the conclusion follows from the data
